claim: GABAARs fracture to both the protoplasmic (P-face) and extracellular (E-face) halves of the plasma membrane.
source: We found a strong positive correlation between P- and E-face gold particle numbers (Figure 1F), demonstrating that GABAARs fracture to both faces of the plasma membrane and the synapse-to-synapse variability in gold particle number is not the consequence of synapse-to-synapse variability in fracturing to E- and P-faces.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a strong positive correlation (Figure 1F) between P-face and E-face gold particle numbers in face-matched mirror replica labeling experiments.

claim: All CA1 pyramidal cell somatic and AIS synapses contain the γ2 subunit.
source: Using replica immunogold labeling, here we show that all CA1 PC somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 and γ2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All CA1 pyramidal cell somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1 subunit.
source: Using replica immunogold labeling, here we show that all CA1 PC somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 and γ2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All CA1 pyramidal cell somatic and AIS synapses contain the α2 subunit.
source: Using replica immunogold labeling, here we show that all CA1 PC somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 and γ2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All CA1 pyramidal cell somatic and AIS synapses contain the β1 subunit.
source: Using replica immunogold labeling, here we show that all CA1 PC somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 and γ2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All CA1 pyramidal cell somatic and AIS synapses contain the β2 subunit.
source: Using replica immunogold labeling, here we show that all CA1 PC somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 and γ2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All CA1 pyramidal cell somatic and AIS synapses contain the β3 subunit.
source: Using replica immunogold labeling, here we show that all CA1 PC somatic and AIS synapses contain the α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 and γ2 subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 90% of CA3 pyramidal cell perisomatic synapses are immunopositive for the α1 subunit.
source: In CA3 PCs, 90% of the perisomatic synapses are immunopositive for the α1 subunit and all synapses are positive for the remaining five subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative SDS-FRL data showing that ~10% of CA3 PC synapses are immunonegative for the α1 subunit.

claim: All CA3 pyramidal cell perisomatic synapses contain the α2, β1, β2, β3, and γ2 subunits.
source: In CA3 PCs, 90% of the perisomatic synapses are immunopositive for the α1 subunit and all synapses are positive for the remaining five subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data.

claim: Somatic synapses form unimodal distributions based on their immunoreactivity for GABAAR subunits.
source: Somatic synapses form unimodal distributions based on their immunoreactivity for these subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by distribution histograms shown in multiple figures (Figures 2H,I, 3H,I, 4H,I, 5H,I).

claim: The α2 subunit densities in somatic synapses facing Cav2.1 (parvalbumin) positive presynaptic active zones are comparable to those facing Cav2.2 (cholecystokinin) positive active zones.
source: The α2 subunit densities in somatic synapses facing Cav2.1 (i.e. parvalbumin) or Cav2.2 (cholecystokinin) positive presynaptic active zones are comparable.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative data from quadruple-labeling experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Perisomatic synapses made by three distinct interneuron types have similar GABAA receptor subunit content.
source: We conclude that perisomatic synapses made by three distinct interneuron types have similar GABAA receptor subunit content.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the collective data from SDS-FRL experiments comparing subunit content across different synapse types.

claim: The number of gold particles for both NL-2 and the γ2 subunit in AIS and somatic synapses shows a positive correlation with the synaptic area.
source: The number of gold particles for both NL-2 and the γ2 subunit in AIS and somatic synapses shows a positive correlation with the synaptic area (Figures 2E,F, 3E,F), demonstrating that the main source of variability in the postsynaptic receptor number is the variance in the synaptic area.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 2E,F and 3E,F, demonstrating positive correlations between gold particle numbers and synaptic area.

claim: CA1 AIS synapses are significantly smaller than CA1 somatic and CA3 AIS synapses.
source: Statistical comparisons of the four compartments revealed that CA1 AIS synapses are significantly smaller than CA1 somatic and CA3 AIS synapses (Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparisons of synaptic areas shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Normalized γ2 subunit densities were significantly higher in CA3 and CA1 AIS synapses than in somatic synapses of both regions.
source: In contrast, we found that normalized γ2 subunit densities were significantly higher in CA3 and CA1 AIS synapses than in somatic synapses of both regions (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparisons of normalized γ2 subunit densities shown in Figure 3K.

claim: All GABAergic synapses on hippocampal PC soma and AIS contain the γ2 subunit and NL-2.
source: These results demonstrate that all GABAergic synapses on the soma and AIS of both CA1 and CA3 PCs contain the γ2 subunit and NL-2, enabling their use as GABAergic synapse-specific markers.
evidence: The claim is supported by face-matched mirror replica labeling experiments showing co-localization of NL-2 and γ2 subunit in all examined synapses.

claim: All somatic and AIS synapses are immunopositive for the α1 subunit on CA1 PCs.
source: This sampling method resulted in an unbiased synapse population and revealed that all somatic and AIS synapses are immunopositive for the α1 subunit on CA1 PCs (Figure 4I), but that ~10% of CA3 PC synapses are immunonegative for the α1 subunit (AIS: 4 out of 50; soma: 44 out of 402; Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of α1 subunit immunogold labeling in CA1 PC synapses shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Approximately 10% of CA3 PC perisomatic synapses are immunonegative for the α1 subunit.
source: This sampling method resulted in an unbiased synapse population and revealed that all somatic and AIS synapses are immunopositive for the α1 subunit on CA1 PCs (Figure 4I), but that ~10% of CA3 PC synapses are immunonegative for the α1 subunit (AIS: 4 out of 50; soma: 44 out of 402; Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing 4 out of 50 AIS synapses and 44 out of 402 somatic synapses were immunonegative for α1 in CA3 PCs.

claim: The α1 subunit density was twice as high in CA1 compared to CA3 perisomatic synapses.
source: The density of the α1 subunit was twice as high in CA1 compared to CA3 perisomatic synapses (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of normalized α1 subunit densities shown in Figure 4G.

claim: No immunonegative synapse was found for the α2 subunit in any of the examined compartments.
source: Despite these quantitative differences in the overall densities, no immunonegative synapse was found in any of these compartments.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of α2 subunit immunogold labeling showing all synapses were immunopositive.

claim: The α2 subunit density was significantly lower in CA1 somatic synapses compared to the other three synapse populations.
source: Next we assessed the α2 subunit content of synapses (Figure 5) and found a significantly lower density in CA1 somatic synapses compared to the other three synapse populations (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The α2 subunit density was significantly lower in CA3 somatic synapses than in CA1 AIS synapses.
source: Furthermore, the α2 subunit density was significantly lower in CA3 somatic synapses than in CA1 AIS synapses (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparisons shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There is no negative correlation between α1 and α2 subunit densities in individual CA1 and CA3 PC somatic synapses.
source: Comparison of the somatic α1 and α2 subunit densities showed a lack of negative correlation in both the CA1 and CA3 areas (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D, which found no significant correlation between α1 and α2 densities.

claim: The variability in the α1:α2 ratio is similar between AIS and somatic synapses in both CA1 and CA3 regions.
source: However, our analysis revealed a lack of significant difference between the α1:α2 in AIS and somatic synapses in the CA1 (p=0.347, Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by multiple comparisons of mean ranks) and CA3 (p=0.053) regions (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference in α1:α2 ratios between AIS and somatic synapses, as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: All AIS and somatic synapses in the CA3 and CA1 regions contain the β1, β2, and β3 subunits.
source: Quantitative analysis of the reactions revealed that all AIS and somatic synapses in the CA3 and CA1 regions contained the β1, β2, and β3 subunits and that somatic synapses formed unimodal distributions based on their β subunit densities (Figures 8E,F; 9E,F; 10E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative SDS-FRL immunogold labeling data for β1, β2, and β3 subunits shown in Figures 8, 9, and 10.

claim: Somatic synapses form unimodal distributions based on their β subunit densities.
source: Quantitative analysis of the reactions revealed that all AIS and somatic synapses in the CA3 and CA1 regions contained the β1, β2, and β3 subunits and that somatic synapses formed unimodal distributions based on their β subunit densities (Figures 8E,F; 9E,F; 10E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by distribution histograms for β1, β2, and β3 subunits shown in Figures 8E,F; 9E,F; and 10E,F.

claim: Immunofluorescent labeling in low-pH fixed tissue revealed the presence of α1, α2, β1, β2, β3, and γ2 subunits in virtually all AIS and somatic synapses of the CA3 region.
source: Immunofluorescent labeling of the six major GABAAR subunits with a low-pH-based fixation protocol revealed the presence of α1, α2, β1, β2, β3, and γ2 subunits in virtually all AIS and somatic synapses of the CA3 region, consistent with the EM SDS-FRL results.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 11, which demonstrates co-localization of all six subunits with synaptic markers.

claim: The subunit composition of GABAARs in somatic and AIS synapses is very similar in both CA1 and CA3 PCs.
source: Our quantitative SDS-FRL experiments revealed that the subunit composition of GABAARs in somatic and AIS synapses is very similar in both CA1 and CA3 PCs.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement in the Discussion section, supported by the collective quantitative data from SDS-FRL experiments.

claim: The prominent demarcation of CA3 PC AISs for the α2 subunit is due to the larger synaptic size and large synaptic coverage of AISs, not unique α2 subunit predominance.
source: The fact that CA3 AISs appear strongly demarcated for the α2 subunit, which has similar densities in somatic and AIS synapses, indicates that the larger synaptic size and the large synaptic coverage of AISs are primarily responsible for their apparent predominance for α2 subunit labeling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that α2 densities are similar in somatic and AIS synapses, yet AISs appear more strongly labeled in fluorescence microscopy.

claim: AAC- and basket cell-evoked IPSCs should have similar decay kinetics based on similar postsynaptic GABAAR subunits.
source: The similar postsynaptic GABAAR subunits in AIS and somatic synapses indicate that AAC- and basket cell-evoked IPSCs should have similar decay kinetics.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the finding of similar GABAAR subunit composition in AIS and somatic synapses, combined with knowledge that subunit composition determines IPSC kinetics.

claim: Szabo et al. (2010) found that AAC-evoked postsynaptic responses had slower decay than basket cell-evoked responses under normal conditions.
source: Szabo et al. (2010) compared the decay times of IPSCs evoked by PV+ and CCK+ basket cells and AACs and found that the AAC-evoked postsynaptic response had a slower decay.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Szabo et al. (2010).

claim: Under low release probability conditions where no spillover is expected, AAC- and basket cell-evoked IPSCs have similar decay times.
source: However, based on the work of Overstreet and Westbrook (2003), demonstrating extensive spillover between the axon terminals of AACs that slows IPSCs, Szabo et al. (2010) examined the decay of AAC-evoked IPSCs under low release probability conditions where no spillover is expected and found similar decay times of AAC- and basket cell-evoked IPSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Overstreet and Westbrook (2003) and Szabo et al. (2010).

claim: AAC and basket cells activate GABAARs with similar subunit composition on their postsynaptic PCs.
source: All of these results are consistent with the notion that AAC and basket cell activate GABAARs with similar subunit composition on their postsynaptic PCs, predicting similar postsynaptic regulation and pharmacological properties.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the collective data from the study and previous functional studies.

claim: Fast-spiking (PV+) basket cells activate α2 subunit-containing GABAARs in CA3 PCs.
source: Using transgenic animals with a point mutation rendering the α2 subunit insensitive to benzodiazepines, Heistek et al. (2013) demonstrated that fast-spiking (PV+) basket cells activate α2 subunit-containing GABAARs in CA3 PCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Heistek et al. (2013).

claim: The release of GABA from CCK+ basket cell axon terminals is mediated by Cav2.2 voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: An elegant example of their molecular specialization is that the release of GABA from the axon terminals of CCK+ basket cells is mediated by Cav2.2 voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and is under the control of CB1 cannabinoid receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Freund and Katona (2007).

claim: The release of GABA from CCK+ basket cells is under the control of CB1 cannabinoid receptors.
source: An elegant example of their molecular specialization is that the release of GABA from the axon terminals of CCK+ basket cells is mediated by Cav2.2 voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and is under the control of CB1 cannabinoid receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Freund and Katona (2007).

claim: The release of GABA from PV+ basket cells is exclusively mediated by Cav2.1 channels.
source: In contrast, the release of GABA from PV+ basket cells is exclusively mediated by Cav2.1 channels and is regulated by m2 muscarinic and μ opiate receptors (reviewed by Freund and Katona, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Freund and Katona (2007).

claim: The release of GABA from PV+ basket cells is regulated by m2 muscarinic and μ opiate receptors.
source: In contrast, the release of GABA from PV+ basket cells is exclusively mediated by Cav2.1 channels and is regulated by m2 muscarinic and μ opiate receptors (reviewed by Freund and Katona, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Freund and Katona (2007).

claim: PC somatic synapses facing PV+ axon terminals contain mainly α1 subunit-containing GABAARs.
source: It was shown that PC somatic synapses facing PV+ axon terminals contain mainly α1 subunit-containing GABAARs (Klausberger et al., 2002) whereas somatic synapses opposite to CCK+ boutons and AIS synapses predominantly contain GABAARs incorporating the α2 subunit (Nusser et al., 1996; Fritschy et al., 1998; Nyiri et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klausberger et al. (2002).

claim: Somatic synapses opposite to CCK+ boutons predominantly contain GABAARs incorporating the α2 subunit.
source: It was shown that PC somatic synapses facing PV+ axon terminals contain mainly α1 subunit-containing GABAARs (Klausberger et al., 2002) whereas somatic synapses opposite to CCK+ boutons and AIS synapses predominantly contain GABAARs incorporating the α2 subunit (Nusser et al., 1996; Fritschy et al., 1998; Nyiri et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nusser et al. (1996), Fritschy et al. (1998), and Nyiri et al. (2001).

claim: AIS synapses predominantly contain GABAARs incorporating the α2 subunit.
source: It was shown that PC somatic synapses facing PV+ axon terminals contain mainly α1 subunit-containing GABAARs (Klausberger et al., 2002) whereas somatic synapses opposite to CCK+ boutons and AIS synapses predominantly contain GABAARs incorporating the α2 subunit (Nusser et al., 1996; Fritschy et al., 1998; Nyiri et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nusser et al. (1996), Fritschy et al. (1998), and Nyiri et al. (2001).

claim: Synaptic GABAARs with distinct subunit compositions confer different decay kinetics to the postsynaptic responses.
source: Synaptic GABAARs with distinct subunit compositions confer different decay kinetics to the postsynaptic responses (Verdoorn et al., 1990; Tia et al., 1996; Lavoie et al., 1997; Vicini, 1999; Bianchi et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating the relationship between GABAAR subunit composition and IPSC kinetics.

claim: The decay time of IPSCs mediated by α2 subunit-containing GABAARs is 3–4-times slower compared to that of IPSCs mediated by α1 subunit-containing GABAARs.
source: The decay time of IPSCs mediated by α2 subunit-containing GABAARs is 3–4-times slower compared to that of IPSCs mediated by α1 subunit-containing GABAARs (Eyre et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eyre et al. (2012).

claim: Fast rising (likely perisomatic) spontaneous IPSCs recorded from PCs have rather uniform decays.
source: However, this is in contrast with the rather uniform decays of fast rising (likely perisomatic) spontaneous IPSCs recorded from PCs (Nusser et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nusser et al. (2001).

claim: The density of functional GABAARs was estimated to be ~1200 receptors per µm2 in cerebellar stellate cell synapses.
source: The density of functional GABAARs was estimated to be ~1200 receptors per µm2 in cerebellar stellate cell synapses (Nusser et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nusser et al. (1997).

claim: The highest labeling efficiency of the postembedding immunogold method for AMPA and GABAARs localization was estimated to be around 30–40%.
source: The highest labeling efficiency of the postembedding immunogold method for AMPA and GABAARs localization was estimated to be around 30–40% (Nusser et al., 1997, 1998), but it could be as high as 90–100% with SDS-FRL (Tanaka et al., 2005; Lorincz and Nusser, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nusser et al. (1997, 1998).

claim: The labeling efficiency with SDS-FRL could be as high as 90–100%.
source: The highest labeling efficiency of the postembedding immunogold method for AMPA and GABAARs localization was estimated to be around 30–40% (Nusser et al., 1997, 1998), but it could be as high as 90–100% with SDS-FRL (Tanaka et al., 2005; Lorincz and Nusser, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tanaka et al. (2005) and Lorincz and Nusser (2010).

claim: Face-matched mirror replica labeling for the γ2 subunit revealed around 800 gold / μm2 on the E-face and 250 gold / μm2 on the P-face.
source: Our face-matched mirror replica labeling for the γ2 subunit revealed around 800 gold / μm2 on the E- and 250 gold / μm2 on the P-face, resulting in ~1050 gold in every μm2 of postsynaptic membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from face-matched mirror replica labeling experiments.

claim: An almost 90% labeling efficiency can be calculated in the best reactions if a similar GABAAR density characterizes hippocampal perisomatic synapses to that found in cerebellar stellate cells.
source: If a similar GABAAR density characterizes hippocampal perisomatic synapses to that found in cerebellar stellate cells, an almost 90% labeling efficiency can be calculated in our best reactions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the gold particle density obtained in the study with the known receptor density in cerebellar stellate cells.

claim: SDS-FRL has a superior sensitivity compared to postembedding labeling.
source: Thus, SDS-FRL has a superior sensitivity compared to postembedding labeling, the only other localization technique that allows the visualization of receptors and ion channels embedded in dense protein matrices found in e.g. postsynaptic membranes or AISs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of labeling efficiencies between SDS-FRL and postembedding methods, supported by citations.

claim: Hippocampal PV+ and CCK+ basket cells receive similar excitatory inputs and provide their output to the same subcellular domains of PCs.
source: For example, hippocampal PV+ and CCK+ basket cells receive similar excitatory inputs and provide their output to the same subcellular domains of PCs (somata and proximal dendrites), but fire in different phases of theta oscillations, and only PV+ cells are active during sharp wave-associated ripples (Klausberger et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klausberger et al. (2005).

claim: PV+ and CCK+ basket cells fire in different phases of theta oscillations.
source: For example, hippocampal PV+ and CCK+ basket cells receive similar excitatory inputs and provide their output to the same subcellular domains of PCs (somata and proximal dendrites), but fire in different phases of theta oscillations, and only PV+ cells are active during sharp wave-associated ripples (Klausberger et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klausberger et al. (2005).

claim: Only PV+ basket cells are active during sharp wave-associated ripples.
source: For example, hippocampal PV+ and CCK+ basket cells receive similar excitatory inputs and provide their output to the same subcellular domains of PCs (somata and proximal dendrites), but fire in different phases of theta oscillations, and only PV+ cells are active during sharp wave-associated ripples (Klausberger et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klausberger et al. (2005).

claim: External tufted cells of the main olfactory bulb express the α1 and α3 subunits and display small synapse-to-synapse, but large cell-to-cell variability in the α1:α3 ratio.
source: A study from our laboratory demonstrated that external tufted cells of the main olfactory bulb express the α1 and α3 subunits and display small synapse-to-synapse, but large cell-to-cell variability in the α1:α3 ratio (Eyre et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Eyre et al. (2012).

claim: The decay kinetics of IPSCs recorded from tufted cells have small within-cell, but large cell-to-cell variability.
source: Consistent with this, the decay kinetics of IPSCs recorded from tufted cells have small within-cell, but large cell-to-cell variability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the finding of small synapse-to-synapse but large cell-to-cell variability in α1:α3 ratios in tufted cells, combined with knowledge that subunit composition determines IPSC kinetics.

claim: Hippocampal PCs exhibit moderate synapse-to-synapse, but small cell-to-cell variability in the α1:α2 ratio.
source: Here, we found that hippocampal PCs exhibit moderate synapse-to-synapse, but small cell-to-cell variability in the α1:α2.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of α1:α2 ratios shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There is very small cell-to-cell variability in mIPSC decay times recorded from PCs.
source: This is in agreement with the very small cell-to-cell variability in mIPSC decay times recorded from PCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the finding of small cell-to-cell variability in α1:α2 ratios, combined with knowledge that subunit composition determines IPSC kinetics.

claim: Distinct neuronal types use unique strategies for expressing multiple synaptic GABAAR α subunit isoforms with either a variable or constant ratio from synapse-to-synapse and cell-to-cell.
source: Thus, our analysis of the ratios of two α subunits in two cell types demonstrate that distinct neuronal types use unique strategies for expressing multiple synaptic GABAAR α subunit isoforms with either a variable or constant ratio from synapse-to-synapse and cell-to-cell, allowing them to fulfill individual cellular requirements in network dynamics.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparing the variability patterns of α subunit ratios in tufted cells versus hippocampal PCs.

claim: The β2 subunit has a critical role in a form of inhibitory synaptic plasticity observed at a cerebellar synapse.
source: Furthermore, the β2 subunit has a critical role in a form of inhibitory synaptic plasticity observed at a cerebellar synapse (He et al., 2015), demonstrating its crucial involvement in setting the synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to He et al. (2015).

claim: Different β subunit isoforms are responsible for the polarized distribution of recombinant GABAARs.
source: Furthermore, almost nothing is known about the quantitative relationship between different β subunits in PC somatic and AIS synapses, although different β subunit isoforms were shown to be responsible for the polarized distribution of recombinant GABAARs (Connolly et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Connolly et al. (1996).

claim: There are multiple types of INs that innervate the perisomatic region of PCs (axo-axonic cell, parvalbumin-expressing basket cells, and cholecystokinin-expressing basket cells).
source: However, there are multiple types of INs that innervate the perisomatic region of PCs (axo-axonic cell (AAC), parvalbumin- (PV+) and cholecystokinin-expressing (CCK+) basket cells), yet participate in distinct network computations as inferred from their differential firing during oscillations (Klausberger et al., 2003, 2005; Varga et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing these interneuron types.

claim: Perisomatic-targeting interneurons participate in distinct network computations as inferred from their differential firing during oscillations.
source: However, there are multiple types of INs that innervate the perisomatic region of PCs (axo-axonic cell (AAC), parvalbumin- (PV+) and cholecystokinin-expressing (CCK+) basket cells), yet participate in distinct network computations as inferred from their differential firing during oscillations (Klausberger et al., 2003, 2005; Varga et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klausberger et al. (2003, 2005) and Varga et al. (2012).

claim: Distinct IN types play unique roles in memory formation and retrieval, network oscillations and sensory perception.
source: Recent in vivo electrophysiological, imaging and optogenetic studies demonstrated that distinct IN types play unique roles in memory formation and retrieval, network oscillations and sensory perception (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Lovett-Barron et al., 2012; Varga et al., 2012; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating the diverse roles of interneuron types.

claim: Most central neurons express multiple GABAAR subunit types.
source: Most central neurons express multiple GABAAR subunit types (Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Pirker et al., 2000) and their individual synapses contain many different subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fritschy and Mohler (1995) and Pirker et al. (2000).

claim: Individual synapses contain many different GABAAR subunits.
source: Most central neurons express multiple GABAAR subunit types (Fritschy and Mohler, 1995; Pirker et al., 2000) and their individual synapses contain many different subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on the data presented in the study showing co-localization of multiple subunits in individual synapses.

claim: The fracturing plane often crosses the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes with transmembrane proteins remaining either in the protoplasmic (P-face) or extracellular (E-face) half of the membrane.
source: The basic principle of SDS-FRL is that following random fracturing of frozen tissue, the fracturing plane often crosses the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes with transmembrane proteins remaining either in the protoplasmic (P-face) or extracellular (E-face) half of the membrane (Fujimoto, 1995; Rash et al., 1998; Masugi-Tokita and Shigemoto, 2007).
evidence: The claim describes the basic principle of SDS-FRL and is supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: If an antibody recognizes intracellular epitope(s), specific immunolabeling will be detected in the P-face of the membrane.
source: If an antibody recognizes intracellular epitope(s), specific immunolabeling will be detected in the P-face of the membrane, whereas extracellular epitopes will be visualized on the E-face.
evidence: The claim describes a fundamental principle of SDS-FRL methodology.

claim: Extracellular epitopes will be visualized on the E-face.
source: If an antibody recognizes intracellular epitope(s), specific immunolabeling will be detected in the P-face of the membrane, whereas extracellular epitopes will be visualized on the E-face.
evidence: The claim describes a fundamental principle of SDS-FRL methodology.

claim: NL-2 is a GABAergic synapse-specific cell adhesion molecule.
source: To avoid complications arising from potential competition between different antibodies on the same replica, the mirror replica method was used for the co-localization of the γ2 subunit and neuroligin-2 (NL-2), a GABAergic synapse-specific cell adhesion molecule (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Varoqueaux et al. (2004) elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: GABAergic synapses appear as small membrane patches rich in IMPs on the P-face of the plasma membrane.
source: A GABAergic synapse-specific adhesion molecule (Varoqueaux et al., 2004), NL-2, was used to identify AIS and somatic synapses on the P-face of the plasma membrane, where GABAergic synapses appear as small membrane patches rich in IMPs (Kasugai et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kasugai et al. (2010).

claim: There was large variability in the area of AIS and somatic synapses.
source: There was large variability in the area of AIS and somatic synapses (CA3 AIS: CV = 0.6, n = 161; CA1 AIS: CV = 0.4, n = 164; CA3 soma: CV = 0.7, n = 1105; CA1 soma: CV = 0.7, n = 767).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing coefficients of variation for synaptic areas.

claim: The similar variability in α2 subunit densities in AIS and somatic synapses suggests the lack of multiple somatic synapse populations based on their GABAAR α2 subunit content.
source: The similar variability in α2 subunit densities in AIS and somatic synapses (CA3 AIS: CV = 0.3, n = 46, CA3 soma: CV = 0.2, n = 470; CA1 AIS: CV = 0.2, n = 35, CA1 soma: CV = 0.3, n = 222) also suggests the lack of multiple somatic synapse populations based on their GABAAR α2 subunit content.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of similar coefficients of variation in α2 subunit densities across different synapse populations.

claim: The variability in α2 subunit density was similar between Cav2.1+, Cav2.2+, and unidentified synapse populations.
source: The variability in α2 subunit density was also similar between the three synapse populations (CA1 area: Cav2.1+: CV = 0.5; Cav2.2+: CV = 0.4; unidentified: CV = 0.3; CA3 area: Cav2.1+: CV = 0.3; Cav2.2+: CV = 0.3; unidentified: CV = 0.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing similar coefficients of variation across the three synapse populations.

claim: In the CA3 area, the density of α2 subunit in the Cav2.1+ AZ-associated synapses was significantly higher than that in unidentified synapses.
